Dual-frequency ranging

From the figure to the physics

Fig. 1 shows how two pseudorange frequencies cancel a leading ionospheric delay while retaining common range.

To first order, ionospheric code delay varies as 1/f². A lower-frequency pseudorange therefore has a larger positive delay for the same ionospheric conditions. Write P₁ = ρ + b + K/f₁² and P₂ = ρ + b + K/f₂², with all range terms in metres.

Choose α = f₁²/(f₁² − f₂²) and β = −f₂²/(f₁² − f₂²). Their sum is 1, preserving the common geometric range and bias, while α/f₁² + β/f₂² = 0 cancels the leading ionospheric term.

For equal independent per-frequency noise standard deviation σ, the combined noise is σ√(α² + β²). The negative coefficient permits cancellation but also increases noise. Hardware biases, higher-order ionosphere, and other common residuals need their own corrections.

Example

For L1 = 1575.42 MHz and L2 = 1227.60 MHz, α ≈ 2.546 and β ≈ −1.546. The independent equal-noise multiplier is approximately 2.978, so 0.5 m noise on each frequency gives approximately 1.489 m combined noise.

Model and course sources

    Practice

    1. Does this ionosphere-free combination remove a common 3 m clock-distance residual as well?

    Multiply the common term by α + β.

    The 3 m residual remains because α + β = 1. The combination isolates a particular frequency-dependent error rather than canceling every error source.

    2. Why can the combined measurement have greater random noise even though its first-order ionospheric error is smaller?

    Noise variances contain squared coefficients, whose signs disappear.

    Independent noise variances add as α²σ² + β²σ². The opposing signs cancel the correlated 1/f² term but do not cancel independent random noise.
